primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst. Repricing of ad-exposed mega-cap tech after failed relief rally following Fed emergency 50bp cut
secondary_factors: Growing fear COVID would hit advertising budgets especially brand and travel-related ads. Reuters later reported U.S. ad market expected to lose nearly $26B in 2020
store_description: Alphabet sold off because the market stopped treating it as insulated. After the Fed surprise 50bp cut on Mar 3 failed to hold gains investors began discounting a severe ad slowdown. Reuters later reported YouTube brand advertising weakened and the U.S. ad market could shrink 10.6%.

primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst. Same ad-market repricing as GOOG class after failed Fed relief rally
secondary_factors: Travel auto and small-business advertisers expected to pull spending
store_description: Same dynamics as GOOG. Alphabet Class A shares fell 3.5% as investors priced in a severe advertising slowdown after the Fed emergency cut failed to reassure markets. No company-specific headline in the Feb 29 to Mar 3 window.

primary_cause: COVID repricing of Berkshire's economically sensitive portfolio including airlines financials industrials retail and manufacturing
secondary_factors: Airline exposure financial holdings and concern conglomerate structure would not shield from sudden activity shock
store_description: No fresh Berkshire company event in the Mar 1-3 window. The stock fell because Berkshire was effectively a levered bet on the real economy at the moment investors realized the virus shock would hit insurers banks transport industrial production and especially airlines all at once.

primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst. Cyclical enterprise IT and consulting selloff after failed Fed relief rally
secondary_factors: Concern about corporate IT spending freezes as clients pivoted from transformation to liquidity preservation
store_description: No discrete IBM headline before the Mar 3 drop. The move looks consistent with a market reassessment that large enterprise vendors would face slower software services and infrastructure demand if clients pivoted to liquidity preservation which Reuters later confirmed happened.

primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst. Semiconductor and tech de-risking tied to virus spread and supply-chain worries
secondary_factors: General selloff in growth tech and concern enterprise and gaming demand could soften. Record-low Treasury yields worsened risk sentiment
store_description: No company announcement or analyst action explaining NVIDIA's Mar 5 move. The stock fell because investors were dumping semis and high-multiple tech into another COVID scare day with record-low Treasury yields reinforcing fears about both supply disruption and cyclical end demand.

primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst. Valuation-driven software selloff on renewed macro fear
secondary_factors: Rotation out of expensive growth software and concern enterprise deal cycles could slow if companies froze budgets
store_description: No ServiceNow-specific event around Mar 5. Classic high-multiple software derating on a day when virus fears intensified and rates collapsed with investors discounting delayed enterprise implementations and weaker spending visibility.

primary_cause: No Nike-specific headline but anticipation of COVID-driven retail traffic collapse and store closures
secondary_factors: China exposure and global consumer discretionary de-risking. Reuters later reported Nike would close stores across U.S. Canada Western Europe Australia and New Zealand by March 27
store_description: Even without a confirmed Nike headline in the prior 72 hours the market was already pricing in a severe hit to store traffic and wholesale demand. Nike's global brick-and-mortar footprint China exposure and dependence on consumer mobility made it a natural casualty.

primary_cause: Rate collapse and margin pressure fears for banks and brokers. 10-year Treasury yield hit record low around 0.899% on Mar 5
secondary_factors: Rising concern over recession trading and credit stress and broad financial-sector de-risking
store_description: This looks sector-specific rather than generic macro. The Fed surprise 50bp cut on Mar 3 flattened the earnings outlook for interest-sensitive financials and by Mar 5 the 10-year yield had fallen below 0.90% intensifying fears around net interest income credit deterioration and broader recession.

primary_cause: No Facebook-specific headline. Repricing of ad-driven internet names on fear of severe marketing budget cuts
secondary_factors: Travel and brand advertisers pulling back plus broader mega-cap tech de-risking
store_description: No company-specific event for Facebook in the Mar 2-5 window. The drop most likely reflected growing belief that even dominant digital ad platforms would not escape a recessionary ad pullback particularly from travel and brand categories as virus fears accelerated.

primary_cause: No Lowe's-specific headline. Consumer-discretionary and retail-traffic fear
secondary_factors: Housing and remodel demand uncertainty and marketwide selloff in cyclical retailers
store_description: Lowe's drop was tied to the market abruptly pricing in a hit to physical retail traffic and consumer confidence rather than a company-specific event. Even though home improvement later proved relatively resilient on Mar 5 investors were not yet differentiating and were selling retailers with store exposure aggressively.

primary_cause: No discrete McDonald's headline. Restaurant traffic and franchise-sales fears tied to the outbreak
secondary_factors: Broad selloff in consumer names dependent on mobility commuting and international traffic
store_description: No McDonald's-specific catalyst in the immediate window. The move most likely reflected investors pricing in fewer store visits weaker urban and travel traffic and operational disruption risk for a global franchise model as COVID concerns shifted to a broader demand shock.

primary_cause: Fear of collapse in cross-border and travel-related card spending. Reuters later confirmed rapid deterioration in cross-border travel-related spending
secondary_factors: Broader payments-sector derating and recession worries
store_description: Mastercard's business mix made it one of the cleaner COVID transmission stocks. Even without a fresh company announcement the market was already discounting a sharp hit to high-margin cross-border volumes as travel restrictions spread. Reuters later documented collapsing travel-related spend.

primary_cause: No Lockheed-specific catalyst. Broad industrial selloff as COVID recession fears deepened
secondary_factors: Risk-off pressure across aerospace and defense even though defense demand itself was less immediately threatened than commercial aerospace
store_description: No company event explaining Lockheed's drop. The move looks mostly like indiscriminate selling in industrial and aerospace names on a day when investors were dumping cyclical exposure.

primary_cause: No Oracle-specific catalyst. Enterprise IT and cyclical tech de-risking
secondary_factors: Failed Fed-cut rally recession fears and concern that customer tech budgets would tighten
store_description: Oracle's Mar 5 decline appears to have been a macro-driven repricing rather than a reaction to a new headline. Investors were selling software and legacy enterprise tech on fears that a virus-driven slowdown would delay database applications and infrastructure spending.

primary_cause: Industrial-production and global manufacturing slowdown fears. Exposure to energy chemicals metals and cyclical end markets
secondary_factors: No Linde-specific headline. General industrial gas demand softening expected if factories refineries and heavy industry slowed
store_description: Linde's move was tied to a market view that industrial gas demand would soften if factories refineries and heavy industry slowed sharply. No obvious company-specific negative catalyst but LIN was exposed to exactly the kind of abrupt decline in manufacturing activity investors were starting to discount.

primary_cause: No Medtronic-specific headline. Medical-device derating on concern hospitals would defer procedures if COVID worsened
secondary_factors: Broad market selloff and uncertainty around hospital purchasing and elective volumes
store_description: Medtronic's drop appears more anticipatory than reactive to a headline. Investors likely began discounting the risk that hospitals would postpone non-urgent procedures and reallocate resources to pandemic response which would pressure device volumes.

primary_cause: No PepsiCo-specific catalyst. Defensive consumer staples still sold in renewed risk-off wave
secondary_factors: Portfolio-wide deleveraging and concern over away-from-home beverage demand
store_description: PepsiCo looks like one of the names pulled lower mainly by the market regime rather than by new company information. Even defensive staples were not spared on Mar 5 as investors raised cash though Pepsi also had some exposure to foodservice and on-the-go consumption.

primary_cause: Fear of falling rail volumes from weaker industrial output trade and freight demand. FT reported COVID already hitting U.S. rail volumes by Mar 5
secondary_factors: Broad transport and industrial derating
store_description: Union Pacific's selloff fits a straightforward macro thesis: if factories slow consumer demand softens and trade flows weaken carloads fall. FT contemporaneous reporting on rail volumes supports the idea investors were already pricing a meaningful freight downturn.

primary_cause: Heavy exposure to commercial aerospace via Pratt & Whitney and Collins amid fast-deteriorating air-travel outlook. 9.1% drop too severe for random beta
secondary_factors: General aerospace and industrial de-risking plus merger-related uncertainty as Raytheon and United Technologies nearing combination
store_description: RTX's 9.1% drop was too severe to dismiss as random beta. Even before the combined company formally withdrew outlook investors were already pricing in a brutal hit to engine aftermarket and aircraft-system demand as the virus hammered airlines travel bookings and global flying activity.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 5 Starbucks said China same-store sales would fall about 50% in the quarter due to COVID
secondary_factors: Worries that China impact would eventually spread to U.S. and broader global operations. Said no perceptible signs of U.S. impact yet
store_description: Among the Mar 5 names Starbucks has one of the cleanest stock-specific catalysts. The company said China same-store sales for the quarter would fall roughly 50% a major revision for a market that had treated the outbreak as more regionally contained. Investors extrapolated the pain could migrate beyond China.
